newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - "City of Dreadful Night" remakes itself.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - "City of Dreadful Night" remakes itself.

text.p: Kipling called it "The City of Dreadful Night"; Mother Teresa won fame by picking up dying destitutes from its crowded streets; and Dominique Lapierre immortalised its festering slums in "The City of Joy".
A quarter-century ago Calcutta's traffic policemen needed armed bodyguards to thwart urban Maoist guerrillas, and the city was regularly plunged into 12-hour power blackouts.
Today Calcutta, home to over 11 million people, boasts much cleaner streets, uninterrupted electricity, the country's only underground railway system, its only trams, and a rejuvenated economy.

Twenty years after a communist alliance seized power in the eastern state of West Bengal, the success of its main city, Calcutta, has proven that state programmes aimed at improving the lives of the poorest can be combined with a pragmatic investment climate.

Cleaner it may be, but West Bengal, which launched a radical investment programme in 1994, may no longer be a bastion of the main Communist Party of India (Marxist) or CPI(M)'s hammer-and-sickle brand of communism.

A survey published this week in Outlook news magazine said 64 percent of people questioned in the eastern state felt life had improved under the communists, but 60 percent felt it had "moved away from leftist ideals over the years".
The communists built their power on land reforms, the redistribution of farmland among landless sharecroppers.
Today the communists say cleaning up Calcutta is high on their list of priorities.

"Cleaning up Calcutta is not only to attract investment but also to provide a reasonable quality of life to one of the most densely populated cities in the world," said Asim Barman, the commissioner of Calcutta's Municipal Corporation.

The state government has already passed several laws, signed agreements with Japanese companies and formed an action group with major local companies for the development of infrastructure and beautification of the city. POWER GROWS OUT OF THE BARREL OF A CEMENT MIXER
Barman said successful land reforms and an upswing in agricultural production had virtually halted the migration of poor Bengalis from the countryside to the cities.

Official figures show the number of people below the poverty line in West Bengal has declined to 27.6 percent today from 52.2 percent in 1977 when the communists took power, and against a national average of 36 percent.
But Calcutta continues to be a magnet. "We cannot continue to be a dustbin for eastern India," said Barman.
Transport Minister Subhas Chakraborty said authorities were building overpasses, widening roads, and phasing out rickshaws pulled by barefoot migrants from the neighbouring state of Bihar.
Calcuttans are happy.
"Now you can walk on the pavements free of slum-dwellers and hawkers and drive through clean streets," says Sunil Ranjan Chatterjee, 64, a retired bureaucrat.

Mayor Kanti Ganguly, who has earned the nickname "Bulldozer" for his swoops on pavement vendors and garbage piles, vows: "We will make Calcutta the cleanest city in India." PROMISES KEPT, BUT CRITICS SAY REFORMS AT STANDSTILL
Jyoti Basu, the state's 82-year-old chief minister, who will celebrate 20 years at the helm on June 20, said his government had always tried to keep the promises it made to voters then.
"It was not a rosy path but we have not made any false promises and we have taken the common people into confidence on every matter. This is the secret of our success," Basu said.
"It's not that we don't have any differences of opinion among the (leftist) partners. But we have always sorted out the differences through discussions," he said.
But opposition politicians say the land reforms that won the communists their support had virtually ground to a standstill.

"Rampant corruption in local governments and politics in choosing the beneficiaries of reform have created anarchy in rural areas, and this is quite evident from the fact that the communists have lost a number of important rural areas in the 1996 elections," said Somen Mitra, president of the state's main opposition group, the Congress party.

Opposition politicians also charge that the drive to woo major industries has left small, village-based industries in the lurch. Official figures show that unemployment currently stands at 5.4 million in a state population of 68 million.
"The fact remains that about 100,000 small, medium and large scale industries are sick," said Saugata Roy, a Congress legislator and a professor of economics.
